title: Juniper and the Room
premise: Juniper Hale inherits her grandmother Bram's house along with a wall of cassette tapes documenting 'The Night Shift,' a radio show taking calls from the recently dead. When every photograph in the house begins to show an extra empty chair — and then Juniper herself, seated in it — she realizes the room in the photos is real, a place her grandmother escaped in 1974 by leaving someone behind. To free herself, Juniper must return what was taken: a name, a body, and the truth of who Bram left in the chair. The price of survival was never paid, only postponed, and the room has been collecting interest for fifty years. Juniper survives only by breaking the inheritance itself — refusing to pass the debt to anyone else — and the found family she gathers along the way helps her burn the contract, though the last photograph still shows the chair, now empty, waiting.
about_author: Emrys Crane is the pen name of a former late-night radio producer who spent years answering phones for strangers at 3 a.m. and never quite stopped listening for the ones who shouldn't be able to call. They write horror about inheritance, houses, and the terrible arithmetic of what we owe.

chapters.title: Static and Ash
chapters.summary: Juniper Hale arrives at her late grandmother's isolated house to sort the estate, grieving and estranged from her own family. In the basement she finds a wall of labeled cassette tapes: 'The Night Shift, 1974.' Third-person POV from Juniper. Emotional beat: hollow grief sharpening into unease.

chapters.title: The Last Broadcast
chapters.summary: Playing the final tape, Juniper hears her grandmother Bram taking a call from a listener who describes his own funeral, held the week before. The tape ends with a knock on the studio door and Bram whispering 'not yet.' Third-person limited, Juniper. Beat: dread — the inheritance is stranger than a house.

chapters.title: Everything Documented
chapters.summary: Juniper discovers Bram's meticulous ledgers: fifty years of names, dates, and 'settlements,' each entry ending with the phrase 'documentation is a kind of prayer.' One ledger from 1974 is missing its final pages, torn out. Third-person, Juniper. Beat: obsessive curiosity; the grandmother she knew becomes a stranger.

chapters.title: The Extra Chair
chapters.summary: Sorting family photographs, Juniper notices every picture taken in the house's back parlor includes a wooden chair that isn't there — old photos, new photos, even a snapshot from her phone yesterday. In the newest one, the chair faces the camera. Third-person, Juniper. Beat: the horror turns personal and visual.

chapters.title: Neighbor at the Fence
chapters.summary: Juniper meets Odile, an elderly neighbor who knew Bram and goes pale at the word 'chair.' Odile warns her not to sit in the parlor after dark and mentions 'the girl who stayed' in 1974, then refuses to say more. Third-person, Juniper with Odile scene. Beat: first ally, first closed door.

chapters.title: Calls Incoming
chapters.summary: The house's dead landline begins ringing at 2:14 a.m. When Juniper answers, callers ask for Bram — and describe the parlor from inside it, the chair beside them, always one seat empty. Third-person, Juniper. Beat: the room is reaching out; she is already on its list.

chapters.title: Seated
chapters.summary: Juniper wakes to find a new photograph on her nightstand: herself, asleep, sitting in the parlor chair that does not exist. The chair in the picture is no longer empty. Third-person, Juniper. Beat: terror — the room has begun collecting her in advance.

chapters.title: What Bram Took
chapters.summary: Behind a false panel Juniper finds the torn 1974 ledger pages: Bram survived the room by offering it her sister, Lorraine, whose name was struck through and rewritten as 'paid in full.' Third-person, Juniper. Beat: revulsion and grief; inheritance revealed as theft.

chapters.title: The Girl Who Stayed
chapters.summary: Juniper tracks down Odile's account: Lorraine Dunmore vanished in 1974, officially a runaway, and Bram never spoke her name again. Odile finally admits the parlor was always 'thin.' Third-person, Juniper and Odile. Beat: the family myth collapses; resolve hardens into purpose.

chapters.title: Found Family, Assembled
chapters.summary: Unable to face it alone, Juniper calls the two people who answer: Marcus, a grief counselor who once called the Night Shift, and Priya, an archivist fascinated by the tapes. The three begin cataloguing the ledgers together. Third-person, ensemble. Beat: warmth against dread — the theme of found family takes root.

chapters.title: Priya's Theory
chapters.summary: Priya identifies the pattern: every 'settlement' in the ledgers is a substitution, and substitutions expire. The room accepts a name, then a body, then a keeper. Bram's fifty years of documentation were payments keeping the contract current. Third-person, Priya-led. Beat: the rules surface; hope and horror in equal measure.

chapters.title: The Keeper's Chair
chapters.summary: Marcus, sitting vigil in the parlor against Juniper's wishes, falls asleep and wakes inside the photograph — he describes the room from within, the wallpaper breathing, the other seated figures turning to look at him. Third-person, Marcus. Beat: first direct contact; the room is populated.

chapters.title: Withdrawal
chapters.summary: Marcus returns but is fading — photographs of him blur, callers on the dead line ask for him by name, and he begins remembering a childhood in the parlor that never happened. Third-person, Marcus. Beat: the price of survival made flesh; guilt lands on Juniper.

chapters.title: Bram's Confession Tape
chapters.summary: A hidden reel surfaces: Bram's voice in 1999, confessing she chose Lorraine because the room demanded 'blood of the keeper,' and that she documented everything not as prayer but as penance that never worked. Third-person, Juniper listening. Beat: the grandmother becomes tragic, not monstrous.

chapters.title: The Room Wants a Keeper
chapters.summary: The parlor door, sealed since Juniper arrived, stands open. Inside, the chair is real, and every photograph in the house now shows Juniper in it, awake, looking out. The room isn't collecting her — it's offering her Bram's old job. Third-person, Juniper. Beat: the trap's true shape revealed.

chapters.title: Lorraine's Voice
chapters.summary: On the dead line, a caller who never gives a name hums a lullaby from the ledger margins. Juniper realizes Lorraine is still in the room — not consumed but kept, the anchor of the whole contract. Third-person, Juniper. Beat: the debt has a face; mercy enters the plan.

chapters.title: Terms of Return
chapters.summary: Priya deciphers the ledger's final cipher: the contract can be voided only by returning what was taken — Lorraine's name spoken back to her by blood, inside the room, before the next settlement date: the anniversary, three days away. Third-person, Priya. Beat: a plan with a deadline.

chapters.title: The Anniversary
chapters.summary: Marcus, half-claimed already, insists on coming; Odile arrives uninvited with salt and a 1974 parish record. The four prepare the parlor as the house grows hostile — doors vanishing, photographs multiplying, the phone ringing continuously. Third-person, ensemble. Beat: found family choosing danger together.

chapters.title: Inside
chapters.summary: Juniper enters the room at 2:14 a.m. It is larger than the house, lined with seated figures from every settlement, Lorraine at the center, young and exhausted. The chair waits for Juniper. She speaks Lorraine's name as blood kin, offering it back. Third-person, Juniper. Beat: climax — the offer and the room's refusal.

chapters.title: The Refusal
chapters.summary: The room counters: it will release Lorraine only if a keeper remains. Juniper refuses to substitute anyone — not herself, not Marcus, not a future heir — and tears the ledger pages, declaring the inheritance broken. The seated figures rise. Bram's tapes, playing in the hall, become a chorus of testimony. Third-person, Juniper. Beat: the price of survival finally paid in truth, not flesh.

chapters.title: Empty Chair
chapters.summary: Dawn. The parlor is a small, ordinary room. Lorraine is gone — released, Odile confirms, dying peacefully that morning with her name on her lips. Marcus's photographs sharpen. The house is quiet for the first time in fifty years. Third-person, ensemble. Beat: grief and relief braided together.

chapters.title: The Last Entry
chapters.summary: Weeks later, Juniper writes the final line in Bram's ledger — not a settlement, but a record: 'The debt ends with me.' She keeps the house with Marcus and Priya, answers no dead calls, and burns the tapes at Lorraine's grave. One photograph remains on the wall: the chair, empty, in a room with no door. Third-person, Juniper. Beat: resolution — survival as choice, not inheritance.
